steps.say: A newborn loses heat astonishingly fast because the skin surface is huge compared with the tiny body, there is almost no insulating fat, and water evaporates constantly from the skin. To stay warm the baby burns fuel without shivering, which uses extra oxygen. A heated isolette holds the core between thirty six and thirty seven point five degrees so that warming never competes with breathing.
steps.tx: Newborns lose heat through a large **surface area** (skin exposure) with little **subcutaneous fat** (insulating layer) and high **insensible loss** (silent water evaporation). They answer with **nonshivering thermogenesis** (heat production without shivering) that raises oxygen demand, so a thermoregulated **isolette** (heated cot) holds core temperature between **36** (thirty six) and **37.5** (thirty seven point five) degrees.

steps.say: Before birth the lungs are bypassed almost completely. Blood crosses from right to left through the hole between the atria and through the vessel joining the lung artery to the body artery. With the first breath the atrial flap shuts, lung vessels relax, flow to the lungs surges, and rising oxygen closes the connecting vessel.
steps.tx: Fetal blood bypasses the lungs through the **foramen ovale** (atrial hole) and the **ductus arteriosus** (lung-to-body artery link). After the first breath the foramen ovale closes while falling **pulmonary vascular resistance** (lung vessel tightness) raises **pulmonary flow** (lung blood volume), and the ductus shuts as oxygen climbs.

steps.say: The picture shows the three structures that must all switch correctly at birth. The airway is narrowest at the ring below the voice box, the duct between the lung and body arteries must close, and the diaphragm must move down with every breath. When any one of them fails, the baby stays blue despite oxygen.
steps.tx: **Neonatal transition** (birth circulation switch) moves blood from placental to lung gas exchange in minutes. The **ductus arteriosus** (arterial shunt) and **foramen ovale** (atrial shunt) close, **pulmonary vascular resistance** (lung circuit pressure) falls, and the **diaphragm** (breathing muscle) must descend freely for the first breaths to inflate the lung.

vis.alt: Medical illustration of neonatal airway anatomy, ductus arteriosus shunt, and diaphragmatic hernia.
vis.caption: Neonatal airway, ductal shunt and diaphragmatic hernia. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: When the lung vessels refuse to relax, blood keeps skipping the lungs and the baby stays blue. Low oxygen and acid blood tighten those vessels further, locking in the shortcut. Breathed nitric oxide relaxes the vessel muscle directly and breaks the cycle.
steps.tx: **Persistent pulmonary hypertension** (locked high lung pressure) keeps a **right to left shunt** (blood skipping the lungs) when **hypoxemia** (low oxygen) and **acidosis** (acid blood) raise **pulmonary vascular resistance** (lung vessel tone). Inhaled **nitric oxide** (vessel-relaxing gas) relaxes vascular **smooth muscle** (vessel wall) and reverses the shunt.

steps.say: A duct that stays open in a premature baby can be closed with medicine. Indomethacin shuts the vessel, avoiding surgery. When drugs fail, the choice is a coil pushed through a catheter or a surgeon tying the vessel through a small chest opening. A heart scan confirms the size of the duct and the direction of flow.
steps.tx: **Indomethacin** (duct-closing drug) closes a **patent ductus arteriosus** (open arterial shunt) in premature infants. Persistent patency moves to **catheter coil** (plug through a tube) occlusion or open surgical **ductal ligation** (vessel tie-off), chosen by size, symptoms and unit expertise. Echocardiography confirms ductal size and **shunt direction** (flow path) before treatment.

steps.say: Watch how the baby breathes and you will spot trouble early. Sixty breaths a minute with flaring nostrils, grunting and ribs pulling in means the lungs are stiff or blocked. A glance at rate, pattern and effort tells you more than any single number.
steps.tx: The healthy newborn breathes **40** (forty) to **60** (sixty) times per minute with a **tidal volume** (each-breath size) of **6** (six) to **10** (ten) mL per kg. **Flaring** (nostril widening), **grunting** (noisy exhaling) and **retractions** (rib indrawing) mark **respiratory distress** (laboured breathing) and demand immediate assessment. The narrow neonatal airway means small **tracheal diameter** (windpipe width) of only **2.5** (two point five) to 4 mm, so **respiratory rate** (breath count) and effort are watched continuously.

vis.alt: Clinical illustration of paediatric breathing inspection, chest shape and symmetry assessment.
vis.caption: Rate, pattern and effort of breathing with chest wall symmetry. Credit: Wikipedia Medical, Pectus carinatum.

steps.say: Tiny babies breathe through the nose and the diaphragm, with almost no help from the rib muscles. A blocked nose or a belly pressing up against the diaphragm leaves them no backup plan. That is why suctioning the nose and keeping the abdomen soft matter so much.
steps.tx: Infants are **obligate nasal breathers** (nose-only airflow) and **diaphragmatic breathers** (belly-driven breaths). A blocked nose or a splinted **diaphragm** (flattened breathing muscle) causes rapid distress with flaring, grunting, **retractions** (chest indrawing) and **cyanosis** (blue colour), so nasal patency and abdominal decompression are priorities.

steps.say: The soap-like coating that keeps the air sacs open is missing in very premature lungs. Without it every breath collapses the sacs and oxygen cannot cross. Giving artificial coating down the breathing tube has transformed survival, while babies who still need oxygen after four weeks have chronic lung disease.
steps.tx: **Surfactant** (air-sac soap) raises **functional residual capacity** (resting lung air), and the **lecithin to sphingomyelin ratio** (maturity test) in amniotic fluid marks lung readiness. Exogenous surfactant improves premature survival, while oxygen need plus radiologic change beyond **28** (twenty eight) days of life defines **bronchopulmonary dysplasia** (chronic lung disease).

steps.say: The newborn heart cannot squeeze harder, only faster, depending entirely on rate. Output climbs with rate, not with each beat, so a climbing pulse and slow refill warn first. Cold pale hands with delayed refill mean the tank is empty and fluids must go in.
steps.tx: The neonatal heart raises **cardiac output** (pump flow) by rate rather than stroke volume, so heart rate change and **capillary refill** (skin-blanch test) are the sensitive markers of **volume status** (tank fullness) and tissue perfusion. Tachycardia with delayed refill triggers fluid **resuscitation** (rapid refill).
